Betta Care sheet.

introduction

There are multiple species of Betta. The most common one kept as a pet is the Betta Splenden. In the wild, Betta's are a murky green, blue or red. The colours you see today have come from selective breeding. Betta's originate from Thailand, Malaysia, Vietnam and some parts of China. They would inhabit rice paddi's filled with dense vegetation throughout most of the year and it would only be for 1 or 2 months after the harvest or during periods of drought that they would live in shallow and small spaces of water. But they would more often than not jump out of that water into larger spaces of water. However, this does not apply to domesticated Betta's, especially the Betta Splenden they need plenty of room to swim in and they are not adapted to wild conditions. Betta's have been bred since the 1800's and are popular in the US and Japan.

Tank size and maintainance requirements.

Although relatively small, Betta's need their space. A 2.5 gallon tank is the minimum tank size requirement for a single Betta. (A 10 Litre tank for those in the UK.) Even then your best starting with a 3 or 5 gallon tank to get them started (13-18 Litres) as they like to swim side ways and can swim relatively fast. A 10 gallon is ideal if you want to split the tank and have two, however, a 10 gallon would need to be heavily planted or decorated for the fish to not become stressed out and tank mates would be adviseable here as Fighting Fish love to hide and open spaces can stress them out. (See the tank mates section for more info.)

The water needs to be soft water, Betta's like the water everso slightly acidic. Adding some drift wood to the tank would sort this problem out. The water must be changed weekly. 25% twice a week is recomended. Make sure to add dechlorinator to the water to ensure the chlorine doesn't burn the fishes gills or kill off any good bacteria. Some bacteria is needed in the tank to break down ammonia produced by fish waste. The bacteria breaks it down into nitrites which are less harmful and then even further into nitrates. Nitrates are not harmfull in small doses, which is why the water changes are need to remove the nitrates before they build up to a toxic level. Plants are great for removing nitrates from the water too. A substrate cleaner is advised to clean the subrate at least once a week to remove decaying fish waste or food.

Oxygenation tablets or plants can be use to keep the water oxygenated as the bacteria will also use the oxygen up. This means it is important to clean the gravel regularily to prevent the bacteria from building up and removing the oxygen. Its also important not to over feed because of this.

The water needs to be kept at a constant temperature so it is important to buy a tank heater ideally with a thermostat built in. You can buy some nano tank heaters on amazon for low prices with a built in theromstat for smaller tanks. A thermometer is also necessary to make sure the water stays between 76 and 82 degrees F. (or 25 and 28 degrees C) Betta's are tropical fish so like warmer water.

A filter with a low flowing current is ideal, such as a sponge filter or an internal filter with an adjustable outflow. Biological media is good to support the bacteria which will remove the ammonia. Activated carbon can also be used to remove any chemicals in the water though must be removed if you are treating an ill fish. Fliter media should be changed a minimum of every 4 weeks.

Decoration and lighting.

Betta's have delicate, floppy fins which mean they can get stuck on anything and everything and that they will tear. Plastic plants should be avoided where possible silk plants are a good alternative to plastic ones. Live plants are even better because they oxygenate the water and remove nitrates and they won't rip your bettas fins. Plants like Amazon Swords are great and fairly low maintainance once theyre settled and Moss balls can make your tank look attractive.

Bog wood thats been sanded down is also good for Betta's as they can hide in it and it softens the water. Any sharp rocks cannot be used in the tank unless they are covered with moss or other plant matter, rounded pebbles are great though and can be used to make a cave. Any ornament should not have sharp edges, but should also have spaces to hide in. Betta's are curious fish and like to interact with their environment. They also love to hide. Tall ornaments are ideal as Bettas like to hang around need the surface of the water and this gives them something to land on. Some people have found the Betta Leaf toy to be sucessful.

LED lights can be used to light up your betta tank, though it should be switched on for no more that 10/11 hours a day as the fish need to rest and it could otherwise cause a build up of algae.

Tank Mates and Territory

Finally, Betta's are most solitary fish. So they are happy being by themselves. However, there are great debates over whether the fish can be kept together, but the general rule is they should be kept seperate. If the fish are in a tank larger than 20 gallons, you could have a collection of female bettas together, or have one male with multiple females as long as there is plenty of space for them to avoid each other if they want and lots of places to hide (2.5 gallons per fish, though this is generally not recommended.). Male Bettas cannot be kept with other male Betta's as they will fight and kill each other.

Tank mates of other species which are ideal for Betta's have to be smaller than the Betta. So fish like Tetras and Cloud Minnows are ideal. Also bottome dwelling fish such as Corydoras are also good as well as some species of shrimp. Plecs do not make good tank mates as they produce a lot of waste and can grow very big. The temperment of a Betta is what dictates other species tank mates. Agressive Bettas will not do well with tank mates and other species cannot be added to a tank less than 10 gallons in size
